UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT
FOR THE EASTERN DISTRICT OF VIRGINIA

ALEXANDRIA DIVISION
MARVELLE J. BALLENTINE,
Plaintiff,
V. Case No. 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD
The Honorable Judge

Rossie D. Alston Jr.

KATIE HALL, individually;
NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN;
META PLATFORMS, INC;
and JOHN/JANE DOES 1-6,

Defendants.

EXHIBIT A

PLAINTIFEF’S SUR-REPLY TO DEFENDANT META PLATFORMS, INC.’S
REPLY IN SUPPORT OF MOTION TO DISMISS

Meta’s Reply largely reiterates its opening arguments. One argument appears for the first
time at page 7. Meta now contends that Plaintiff “has not identified any non-speculative
opportunity for him to provide testimony in any action” and that the FAC fails to identify “any
actual testimony in federal court that Plaintiff has or likely will offer.” ECF No. 39 at 7. The First

Amended Complaint alleges precisely what Meta says is absent.

I. META’S NEW ARGUMENT IS CONTRADICTED BY THE FIRST AMENDED
COMPLAINT

Start with the pleading. Paragraph 31 of the FAC alleges:

Plaintiff was a prospective witness in both actions concerning his account history,
the July 4, 2022 enforcement event, the absence of any law-enforcement contact
with Plaintiff, and his damages. Plaintiff expected to testify under oath at deposition
and at trial concerning those subjects.

ECF No. 5 ¥ 31. That paragraph identifies the witness, the actions, the subjects of the
testimony, and the settings in which it was expected to be given.

The FAC then pleads what Defendants sought to do about that testimony and what they
knew. The purpose of the alleged understanding was “to deter Plaintiff, by intimidation, from
continuing to attend the 376 Action and the 286 Action as a party, and from testifying freely, fully,
and truthfully as a prospective witness in those pending federal proceedings, including concerning
the CyberTipline-reporting question.” Id. ¥ 158. The intimidation “was directed both at Plaintiff’s
continued attendance as a party in the two pending federal actions and at Plaintiff’s own
prospective sworn testimony concerning his account, the July 4, 2022 enforcement event, the
absence of any law-enforcement contact with Plaintiff, and his damages.” Id. § 159. And
Defendants “knew that Plaintiff was pro se; that the noticed depositions depended on Plaintiff’s
personal preparation and examination; that the CyberTipline issue was central to the noticed
examinations; and that Plaintiff was a prospective witness concerning his account, the enforcement
event, and his damages.” Id. § 160. Count IV incorporates those allegations, id. { 234, and
separately repeats the alleged purpose and injury, id. {J 237, 239.

Meta’s argument therefore does not identify an omitted allegation. It asks the Court to
disregard an allegation that is already there.

Rule 12(b)(6) does not permit that. The Court “must accept as true all of the factual
allegations contained in the complaint,” and must draw “all reasonable inferences” in Plaintiff’s
favor. E.I. du Pont de Nemours & Co. v. Kolon Indus., Inc., 637 F.3d 435, 440 (4th Cir. 2011); King

v. Rubenstein, 825 F.3d 206, 212 (4th Cir. 2016). Meta cites no authority imposing an additional

requirement that a § 1985(2) plaintiff identify a future testimony event certain or likely to occur.
Meta’s argument instead asks the Court to find that Plaintiff’s expected testimony was unlikely to
happen. But a plaintiff “need not demonstrate that her right to relief is probable or that alternative
explanations are less likely.” Houck v. Substitute Tr. Servs., Inc., 791 F.3d 473, 484 (4th Cir. 2015).
The question “is not whether there are more likely explanations” for the facts alleged. Woods v.
City of Greensboro, 855 F.3d 639, 649-50 (4th Cir. 2017).

The point can be stated simply. Whether Plaintiff ultimately would have testified is a
factual question concerning what later occurred. The Rule 12 question presented by Meta’s new
argument is whether the FAC plausibly alleges that Plaintiff was a prospective witness and that
the alleged object was to deter his testimony. Paragraphs 31 and 158 through 160 expressly plead

those facts.

Il. META USES LATER PROCEDURAL EVENTS TO NEGATE THE
CIRCUMSTANCES ALLEGED TO EXIST WHEN THE CONDUCT OCCURRED

Meta’s argument depends on two events. The first is the dismissal of the 286 Action. The
second is a motion to dismiss now pending in the 376 Action, which Meta says, “if granted, will
entirely dispose of Plaintiff’s claims before discovery commences.” ECF No. 39 at 7. From those
two events Meta concludes that “it is likely that no such potential testimony will ever come to
fruition.” Id.

Both events postdate the conduct alleged. The FAC pleads the circumstances that existed
on April 22, 2026, when the letters issued. Both federal actions were pending. ECF No. 5 { 27.
Plaintiff was a prospective witness in both. Id. ¥ 31. Plaintiff had noticed Accenture’s Rule 30(b)
(6) deposition for April 29 and 30, 2026, with CyberTipline reporting as a matter for examination.

Id. §§ 51-52. Plaintiff had noticed Anderson’s deposition for April 28, 2026. Id. 4 53. Plaintiff had

retained a court reporter and a videographer. Id. 4] 54. The alleged purpose of the understanding
was to deter that prospective sworn testimony. Id. {{ 158-164.

A later procedural development does not erase the circumstances the FAC alleges existed
when Defendants acted. Both actions were then pending. Plaintiff was then a prospective witness
in both. Depositions were then noticed and imminent. Plaintiff then expected to testify under oath
at deposition and trial. The alleged agreement was then directed at deterring that prospective
testimony. The FAC alleges the circumstances that existed when the challenged conduct occurred.
Later procedural developments do not negate those pleaded historical facts on a Rule 12(b)(6)
motion.

Nor can the possibility that a pending Rule 12 motion may later terminate another action
be converted, on this Rule 12 motion, into a factual determination that Plaintiff’s pleaded
prospective testimony was speculative. The 376 Action has not been dismissed. Meta’s prediction
that Plaintiff’s anticipated testimony is unlikely ever to occur remains a prediction about the future
posture of another case. A prediction about the future of another case is not a ground for dismissing
a well-pleaded allegation about the past in this one.

Ill, META’S REPLY ITSELF DEMONSTRATES WHY ITS NEW CERTAINTY
THEORY FAILS

Meta’s Reply addresses the 376 Action twice. Read together, the two passages establish
one thing: the future posture of that action is unresolved.

At pages 3 and 4, answering Plaintiff’s point that the letters displaced the discovery he had
noticed, Meta says that “to the extent any of Plaintiff’s claims in Ballentine 2 survive defendants’
motion to dismiss, Plaintiff can again seek the discovery he claims was ‘displaced’ or ‘substituted’

by the letters.” ECF No. 39 at 3-4. At page 7, answering Plaintiff’s prospective-witness allegation,

Meta says that because the same motion to dismiss is pending, “it is likely that no such potential
testimony will ever come to fruition.” Id. at 7.

Put those statements side by side. On pages 3 and 4, Meta acknowledges that the 376
Action may survive and that discovery may resume. On page 7, Meta relies on the same unresolved
motion to argue that Plaintiff’s potential testimony is unlikely ever to occur. Meta itself recognizes
that the posture of the 376 Action remains unresolved. A pending motion to dismiss therefore
supplies no factual basis at Rule 12 to declare the FAC’s expressly pleaded prospective testimony
nonexistent or insufficiently concrete.

The statute confirms the point. Section 1985(2) addresses a conspiracy to “deter, by force,
intimidation, or threat, any party or witness in any court of the United States from attending such
court, or from testifying to any matter pending therein, freely, fully, and truthfully.” 42 U.S.C. §
1985(2). The statute expressly protects a party or witness from being deterred from testifying to a
matter pending in federal court. The FAC alleges that both matters were pending, ECF No. 5 { 27;
that Plaintiff was a prospective witness who expected to testify under oath at deposition and trial,
id. 431; the subjects of that testimony, id. J 31, 159; and an alleged purpose to deter it, id. {4 158,
237. Meta cites no authority imposing an additional requirement that the FAC identify a future

testimony event certain or likely to occur.

CONCLUSION

Meta’s new argument supplies no basis for dismissal. The FAC expressly pleads Plaintiff’s
prospective-witness status, the subjects of his anticipated sworn testimony, Defendants’
knowledge of that status, and the alleged purpose of deterring that testimony while both federal
actions were pending. The Court should reject the argument first advanced at page 7 of Meta’s

Reply and deny Meta’s Motion to Dismiss.
